content:
# GRADE 7 AGRICULTURE — TOPIC 1: INTRODUCTION TO AGRICULTURE

## 1. Meaning of agriculture
Agriculture is the science, art and business of producing crops and keeping animals for food, raw materials, income and other useful purposes. It includes activities carried out before production, during production and after production, including land preparation, planting, animal husbandry, harvesting, storage, processing, transport and marketing.

Agriculture is both practical and scientific. A farmer observes conditions, makes decisions, uses tools and inputs, keeps records, manages natural resources and evaluates results. Modern agriculture also involves technology, business management, environmental conservation and value addition.

## 2. Importance of agriculture to Zimbabwe
Agriculture is important to the individual, family, community and national economy.

### Food supply
Crops and livestock provide maize, sorghum, millet, wheat, vegetables, fruits, milk, meat, eggs and other foods. Agriculture therefore contributes directly to household and national food security.

### Employment
Agriculture provides work for farmers, farm workers, extension workers, veterinary personnel, agro-dealers, transporters, processors, traders and many other people.

### Income
Farmers sell crops, animals and processed products to obtain money. Agriculture can therefore be run as a household enterprise, school enterprise, cooperative or commercial business.

### Raw materials
Agricultural products supply industries. Cotton can supply textile industries; hides and skins can supply leather industries; tobacco supplies processing industries; oilseeds can supply oil-processing industries; timber and other plant materials have industrial uses.

### Foreign currency and trade
Agricultural commodities can be sold outside the country and can earn foreign currency. Agricultural imports and exports also affect the country's trade.

### Development of rural areas
Agricultural activities support roads, markets, storage facilities, irrigation, processing centres and other services in rural communities.

### Nutritional improvement
Growing a diversity of crops and keeping different livestock can improve the variety and nutritional quality of household diets.

### Environmental stewardship
Good agriculture can protect soil, conserve water, maintain vegetation and reduce environmental damage. Poor farming can cause erosion, pollution, deforestation and loss of soil fertility.

## 3. Branches of agriculture
Branches are specialised areas of agricultural work.

### Crop production
Growing field crops, vegetables, fruits and ornamental plants.

### Animal husbandry
Keeping and managing domestic animals for products such as meat, milk, eggs, wool, hides and skins.

### Veterinary science
The prevention, diagnosis and treatment of animal diseases and the maintenance of animal health.

### Agricultural engineering
Application of engineering principles to farm structures, machinery, tools, irrigation, drainage and other agricultural operations.

### Agricultural economics and agribusiness
Management of farm resources, costs, production, marketing, processing, income and profit.

### Agricultural extension
Providing farmers with information, demonstrations, advice and improved farming practices.

## 4. Types of farming
### Subsistence farming
Production is mainly intended to meet the farmer's household needs. Surplus may be sold or exchanged.

Advantages include household food production and reduced dependence on purchased food. Limitations may include small scale, limited capital and low marketable surplus.

### Commercial farming
Production is mainly intended for sale and profit. It usually involves deliberate planning, market research, investment and record keeping.

### Mixed farming
Crop production and animal husbandry are carried out on the same farm. Crop residues can feed animals, while animal manure can improve crop fields.

### Diversified farming
A farmer produces several different crops and/or animal products. Diversification can spread risk because failure of one enterprise may be partly compensated by another.

### Specialised farming
The farm concentrates mainly on one enterprise or a narrow group of related enterprises. Specialisation can improve efficiency but may increase risk if the main enterprise fails or prices fall.

### Integrated farming
Different enterprises are deliberately linked so that outputs or wastes from one enterprise become useful inputs for another. Examples include using animal manure in crop production and crop residues as livestock feed.

## 5. Factors affecting agricultural production
### Physical factors
Climate, rainfall, temperature, soil type, relief, water availability and pests/diseases influence production.

### Human factors
Population, labour, skills, land ownership, cultural practices, education and management affect agriculture.

### Economic factors
Capital, input prices, product prices, access to credit, markets and transport influence decisions.

### Technological factors
Availability of improved seed, machinery, irrigation, storage, information and processing technology affects productivity.

### Government and institutional factors
Policies, extension services, research, infrastructure, markets and agricultural programmes can influence production.

## 6. Health and safety in agriculture
Agricultural work can involve sharp tools, machinery, animals, chemicals, dust, fire, water and heavy loads.

Important safety measures include:
- Wear appropriate protective clothing and footwear.
- Use tools only for their intended purposes.
- Keep sharp tools properly stored.
- Carry tools safely, with sharp edges controlled.
- Inspect tools before use.
- Keep work areas clean.
- Follow instructions when handling agricultural chemicals.
- Do not eat, drink or smoke while handling chemicals.
- Wash hands after agricultural work.
- Keep children away from dangerous machinery and chemical stores.
- Treat animal bites, cuts and other injuries promptly.
- Store fuels, chemicals and medicines securely and clearly labelled.
- Use correct lifting techniques for heavy loads.
- Keep livestock handling areas secure.

## 7. Agriculture and food security
Food security means people have reliable access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food. Agriculture contributes through increased production, diversification, proper storage, irrigation, conservation, value addition and reduction of post-harvest losses.

## 8. Sustainable agriculture
Sustainable agriculture meets present needs while conserving resources for future production. Practices include crop rotation, soil conservation, water conservation, controlled grazing, organic matter management, appropriate use of fertilisers, integrated pest management and protection of vegetation.

## 9. Indigenous knowledge and technology
Farmers may use locally available materials and traditional knowledge in seed selection, food preservation, weather observation, livestock management, soil management and construction. Indigenous practices should be evaluated for safety, effectiveness and sustainability and can be combined with scientific knowledge.

## 10. Practical activities
A Grade 7 learner should be able to identify local agricultural enterprises, classify farming systems, conduct a simple farm survey, identify agricultural hazards, demonstrate safe tool handling and explain how agriculture contributes to the local community.

## Examination focus
Be prepared to:
- define agriculture;
- state and explain the importance of agriculture;
- name and describe branches of agriculture;
- distinguish subsistence and commercial farming;
- compare mixed, diversified, specialised and integrated farming;
- identify physical, human, economic and technological factors affecting agriculture;
- state health and safety precautions;
- explain the relationship between agriculture, food security and the economy.

# TOPIC 2: CLIMATE AND LAND USE

## 1. Weather and climate
Weather is the condition of the atmosphere at a particular place and time. Climate is the average pattern of weather experienced over a long period.

Agriculture depends strongly on climate because crops and animals have environmental requirements for growth, reproduction and survival.

## 2. Main elements of weather and climate
### Rainfall
Rainfall supplies water for crops, pastures and livestock. Amount, distribution, intensity and reliability all matter. Heavy rainfall over a short period can cause runoff and erosion, while inadequate rainfall can cause drought stress.

### Temperature
Temperature affects seed germination, crop growth, flowering, fruiting and livestock performance. Different crops have different temperature requirements.

### Sunshine
Sunlight supplies energy for photosynthesis. Day length can also influence some plant developmental processes.

### Wind
Wind affects evaporation, pollination, crop lodging and soil erosion. Strong winds can damage crops and structures.

### Humidity
Humidity affects evaporation, plant water loss and conditions favourable for some diseases.

## 3. Factors affecting climate
Altitude, latitude, distance from large water bodies, relief, vegetation and prevailing winds can influence local climate.

## 4. Zimbabwe's agricultural regions
Zimbabwe has natural farming regions with differences in rainfall, temperature, soils and agricultural potential. The broad pattern commonly taught is:
- Region I: high rainfall and generally high agricultural potential.
- Region II: relatively reliable rainfall and favourable conditions for intensive cropping and livestock production.
- Region III: moderate and less reliable rainfall; drought-resistant crops and livestock systems become more important.
- Region IV: low and unreliable rainfall; drought-resistant crops, livestock and irrigation are important.
- Region V: very low and unreliable rainfall; extensive livestock production, wildlife and other drought-adapted activities are important.

The exact suitability of a particular farm depends on local soil, water, altitude, management and other conditions.

## 5. Land use
Land use means the way people use land. Agricultural land can be used for crop production, grazing, orchards, forestry, wildlife, settlements, infrastructure or mixed purposes.

Land should be used according to its capability. A farmer should consider slope, soil depth, drainage, fertility, rainfall and water availability before choosing an enterprise.

## 6. Matching crops to climate
Examples of crop groups include:
- maize and other cereals;
- sorghum and millet in drier conditions;
- legumes such as beans and groundnuts;
- vegetables under suitable moisture conditions;
- fruits and orchard crops in appropriate climates;
- irrigated crops during dry periods.

Choice of crop should consider temperature, rainfall, growing season, soil and market demand.

## 7. Climate hazards
### Drought
A prolonged period of inadequate rainfall can reduce crop yields, pasture and water supplies.

Responses include drought-tolerant crops, early planting where appropriate, water harvesting, irrigation, conservation agriculture, fodder conservation and appropriate livestock numbers.

### Flooding
Excess water can damage crops, wash away soil and spread disease. Measures include drainage, planting on suitable land, maintaining vegetation and avoiding cultivation in flood-prone areas.

### Strong winds
Windbreaks, shelterbelts, appropriate field orientation and maintaining ground cover can reduce wind damage and erosion.

### Frost
Frost can damage sensitive crops. Farmers can choose suitable planting dates and crops and use appropriate protection methods where feasible.

## 8. Land-use planning
Good planning reduces conflict among agricultural, residential, industrial and conservation uses. A farm plan may show fields, livestock units, water sources, roads, buildings, storage areas, gardens and conservation structures.

## 9. Practical activities
Learners can keep a simple weather record, observe rainfall, compare crops suited to different conditions, draw a farm land-use plan and investigate local climate-related agricultural problems.

## Examination focus
Know the difference between weather and climate; name climate elements; explain how rainfall and temperature affect agriculture; describe Zimbabwe's natural farming regions; identify suitable land uses; and suggest responses to drought, floods and wind erosion.

# TOPIC 3: WATER MANAGEMENT

## 1. Importance of water in agriculture
Water is needed for seed germination, photosynthesis, nutrient transport, cooling and growth of plants. Livestock need water for drinking, digestion, body temperature regulation, milk production and general health.

Water is also used for cleaning animal housing, washing equipment, irrigation, processing and other farm activities.

## 2. Sources of agricultural water
Sources include rainfall, rivers, streams, dams, wells, boreholes, springs, tanks and harvested rainwater.

Water sources should be protected from contamination by chemicals, sewage, waste, dead animals and excessive sediment.

## 3. Water quality
Good agricultural water should be reasonably clean and suitable for its intended use. Polluted water may carry pathogens, chemicals or excessive salts.

## 4. Water conservation
Water conservation means using water carefully and reducing unnecessary loss.

Methods include:
- mulching;
- planting vegetation to reduce runoff;
- contouring on appropriate slopes;
- water harvesting;
- repairing leaking pipes and taps;
- irrigation at suitable times;
- using efficient irrigation methods;
- maintaining soil organic matter;
- avoiding unnecessary over-irrigation.

## 5. Water harvesting
Water harvesting is collecting and storing runoff or rainwater for later use.

Examples include roof catchment tanks, small dams, ponds and other suitable storage systems.

Benefits include improved water availability during dry periods, reduced runoff and support for household or agricultural activities.

## 6. Irrigation
Irrigation is the artificial application of water to crops when natural rainfall is insufficient.

Common systems include:
- surface irrigation;
- sprinkler irrigation;
- drip irrigation.

### Surface irrigation
Water is distributed over or along the soil surface. It can be simple but may lose water through evaporation, runoff and deep percolation if poorly managed.

### Sprinkler irrigation
Water is sprayed over crops like rainfall. It can provide relatively uniform application but requires equipment and energy.

### Drip irrigation
Water is delivered slowly near plant roots. It can save water and is useful for vegetables and other crops, but equipment needs care and maintenance.

## 7. Drainage
Drainage is the removal of excess water from soil or land. Poor drainage can cause waterlogging, root damage, nutrient problems and favourable conditions for some diseases.

Drainage methods depend on the site and may include open drains, channels and appropriate land shaping.

## 8. Water pollution
Agricultural water can be polluted by fertiliser runoff, pesticides, animal waste, soil erosion, household waste and sewage.

Prevention includes correct chemical use, proper waste disposal, buffer vegetation, erosion control and protection of water sources.

## 9. Soil moisture
Plants require water in the soil within a suitable range. Too little causes wilting and poor growth; too much can reduce air in soil and damage roots.

Mulching, organic matter, conservation structures and appropriate irrigation can help manage soil moisture.

## 10. Livestock water
Animals should have access to adequate clean water. Water requirements differ with animal type, age, temperature, diet and production level. Watering points should be kept clean and safely designed.

## 11. Practical activities
Learners can identify local water sources, inspect a water point, demonstrate water harvesting, compare irrigation systems, investigate causes of water pollution and design a simple water-conservation project.

## Examination focus
Define water conservation, irrigation and drainage; name water sources; explain why water is important to crops and animals; compare irrigation methods; identify causes and prevention of water pollution; and describe water-harvesting methods.

# TOPIC 4: SOIL MANAGEMENT

## 1. Meaning of soil
Soil is the upper layer of the earth in which plants grow. It contains mineral particles, organic matter, air, water and living organisms.

## 2. Soil formation
Soil develops through weathering of parent rock and the accumulation and decomposition of organic material. Climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time influence soil formation.

### Weathering
Weathering is the breakdown or alteration of rocks at or near the earth's surface.

Types:
- Physical weathering: rock is broken into smaller pieces without changing its chemical composition.
- Chemical weathering: minerals are chemically altered.
- Biological weathering: organisms contribute to the breakdown of rock.

## 3. Soil profile
A soil profile is a vertical section showing different soil horizons.

A simplified profile may contain:
- O horizon: organic material where present.
- A horizon: topsoil, usually containing much organic matter and many roots.
- B horizon: subsoil where materials may accumulate.
- C horizon: partly weathered parent material.
- R horizon: hard underlying rock.

## 4. Soil components
### Mineral matter
Comes mainly from weathered rocks and supplies the physical framework of soil.

### Organic matter
Comes from dead plants and animals and their decomposition. It improves soil structure, water-holding capacity and nutrient supply.

### Soil water
Dissolves nutrients and is absorbed by plant roots.

### Soil air
Provides oxygen needed by roots and soil organisms.

### Soil organisms
Earthworms, bacteria, fungi and other organisms contribute to decomposition, nutrient cycling and soil structure.

## 5. Soil texture
Soil texture refers to the relative proportions of sand, silt and clay particles.

### Sandy soil
Has large particles, drains rapidly and is usually easy to cultivate. It may have low water- and nutrient-holding capacity.

### Clay soil
Has very small particles, holds much water and nutrients but can become sticky when wet and hard when dry. Drainage may be slow.

### Loam soil
Contains a balanced mixture of sand, silt and clay and is often favourable for many crops when well managed.

## 6. Soil structure
Soil structure refers to how soil particles are arranged into aggregates.

Good structure allows water infiltration, drainage, root growth and air movement.

## 7. Soil fertility
Soil fertility is the ability of soil to supply plants with nutrients in suitable amounts and forms.

Important plant nutrients include nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, together with secondary and micronutrients.

### Nitrogen
Supports leafy growth and is important in proteins and other plant compounds.

### Phosphorus
Supports root development and reproductive processes.

### Potassium
Supports general plant functioning, water regulation and crop quality.

## 8. Maintaining soil fertility
Methods include:
- applying well-managed organic manure;
- using appropriate fertilisers;
- crop rotation;
- growing legumes;
- returning suitable crop residues;
- controlling erosion;
- avoiding unnecessary removal of vegetation;
- using conservation agriculture practices.

## 9. Manure and fertilisers
### Organic manure
Includes decomposed animal dung, compost and other organic materials.

Benefits include adding organic matter and nutrients and improving soil physical condition.

### Inorganic fertilisers
Manufactured fertilisers supply specific plant nutrients. They should be applied according to crop and soil requirements to avoid waste, crop damage and environmental pollution.

## 10. Soil acidity and pH
Soil pH describes how acidic or alkaline soil is. Different crops have different preferred pH ranges. Excessive acidity can limit nutrient availability and affect plant growth. Agricultural lime may be used where appropriate to reduce soil acidity.

## 11. Soil erosion
Soil erosion is the removal and transport of soil particles by agents such as water and wind.

Causes include:
- removal of vegetation;
- overgrazing;
- cultivation up and down steep slopes;
- leaving soil bare;
- uncontrolled runoff;
- strong winds.

Effects include loss of fertile topsoil, reduced yields, siltation of water bodies and land degradation.

## 12. Soil conservation
Methods include:
- contour ridges or contour farming;
- grass strips;
- terracing where suitable;
- mulching;
- cover crops;
- crop rotation;
- maintaining vegetation;
- controlled grazing;
- planting windbreaks;
- water-harvesting structures;
- conservation tillage.

## 13. Soil testing
Soil testing helps determine properties such as pH and nutrient status. The results can guide fertiliser and soil-management decisions.

## 14. Practical activities
Learners can compare soil samples by texture, make a simple soil profile observation, test soil where suitable, demonstrate erosion using a simple model, and design a school soil-conservation project.

## Examination focus
Be able to define soil texture, soil structure, weathering, fertility and erosion; state types of weathering; compare sandy, clay and loam soils; identify soil components; explain soil fertility; distinguish manure from fertiliser; and explain causes, effects and control of soil erosion.

# TOPIC 5: PLANTS AND CROP PRODUCTION

## 1. Importance of crop plants
Crop plants provide food, animal feed, fibre, medicines, income, raw materials and environmental benefits.

Major groups include field crops, vegetables, orchard crops and ornamental plants.

## 2. Crop classification
### Field crops
Crops grown on larger areas mainly for food, feed or industrial use. Examples include maize, sorghum, millet, wheat, beans, groundnuts, cotton and tobacco.

### Vegetables
Crops whose leaves, roots, stems, bulbs, flowers, fruits or immature seeds are eaten. Examples include cabbage, rape, onion, carrot, tomato and pumpkin.

### Orchard crops
Fruit-producing plants grown in orchards, such as citrus, mango, guava and other suitable fruit trees.

### Ornamental plants
Plants grown mainly for beauty, landscaping, decoration or aesthetic value.

## 3. Seed selection
Good seed should be mature, viable, healthy, clean and suitable for the local conditions. Farmers should use recommended varieties and obtain seed from reliable sources where possible.

## 4. Germination
Germination is the process by which a viable seed begins to grow into a seedling.

Conditions commonly required include adequate moisture, suitable temperature and oxygen. Some seeds also have specific light or dormancy requirements.

## 5. Nursery production
A nursery is an area where young plants are raised before transplanting or further growth.

Advantages include easier management of seedlings, efficient use of seed and space, and protection of young plants.

A nursery should have suitable soil, water, drainage, protection and appropriate light.

## 6. Land preparation
Land preparation may involve clearing, primary cultivation, secondary cultivation, levelling, ridging or other operations appropriate to the crop and soil.

Good land preparation should support germination, root growth, weed control and water management without causing unnecessary soil degradation.

## 7. Planting
Planting decisions include:
- time of planting;
- spacing;
- depth;
- seed rate;
- method of planting;
- variety;
- soil moisture.

## 8. Crop management
### Weeding
Weeds compete with crops for water, nutrients, light and space and may harbour pests and diseases.

Control methods include hand weeding, hoeing, mulching, crop competition, appropriate cultural practices and, where permitted and properly managed, herbicides.

### Thinning
Removal of excess seedlings to achieve suitable spacing.

### Gap filling
Replacing missing plants so that the stand is reasonably uniform.

### Mulching
Covering soil around plants with suitable material. Benefits can include reduced evaporation, weed suppression, reduced erosion and improved soil condition.

### Fertilisation
Supplying nutrients using organic or inorganic sources according to crop and soil needs.

### Irrigation
Applying water where rainfall is insufficient.

### Staking and training
Supporting or guiding plants that need physical support.

## 9. Crop rotation
Crop rotation is the planned sequence of different crops grown on the same land over successive seasons.

Benefits include improved soil management, breaking some pest and disease cycles, better use of nutrients and reduced dependence on a single crop.

## 10. Monoculture
Monoculture is growing one crop repeatedly or predominantly on the same land. It can simplify management but may increase vulnerability to particular pests, diseases, nutrient depletion and price changes.

## 11. Pests
A pest is an organism that causes economic damage to crops or agricultural products.

Examples include chewing insects such as caterpillars and beetles and sucking pests such as aphids and some bugs.

### Pest-control methods
- cultural control;
- biological control;
- mechanical/physical control;
- chemical control;
- integrated pest management.

Integrated pest management combines appropriate methods and uses chemicals carefully when necessary.

## 12. Crop diseases
Diseases may be caused by fungi, bacteria, viruses and other pathogens. Symptoms can include leaf spots, wilting, rotting, stunting, discolouration and abnormal growth.

Disease management includes healthy seed, sanitation, resistant varieties where available, crop rotation, proper spacing, removal of infected material and appropriate chemical or biological control.

## 13. Harvesting
Harvest at the correct maturity stage for the intended use. Harvesting too early or too late can reduce quality and storage life.

## 14. Post-harvest handling
Important operations include cleaning, grading, sorting, drying, curing where appropriate, packaging and storage.

### Causes of post-harvest losses
- pests;
- rodents;
- mould;
- poor drying;
- mechanical damage;
- poor storage structures;
- excessive moisture;
- poor handling.

## 15. Marketing and value addition
Farm products can be graded, packaged, processed or transformed to increase their value. Examples include drying vegetables, processing fruits, milling grains and packaging produce.

## 16. Practical crop project
A learner should be able to plan a small school garden project: choose a suitable crop, prepare land, plant, manage weeds and pests, record inputs and labour, harvest, evaluate yield and discuss possible marketing.

## Examination focus
Know definitions and differences involving seed, germination, nursery, transplanting, thinning, gap filling, mulching, monoculture and crop rotation. Be able to describe production stages and explain pest, disease, weed and post-harvest management.

# MASTER GRADE 7 AGRICULTURE REVISION

## The eight Grade 7 Agriculture topics
1. Introduction to Agriculture
2. Climate and Land Use
3. Water
4. Soil
5. Plants
6. Animals
7. Farm Implements and Machinery
8. Agribusiness

## High-priority definitions
Agriculture — the science, art and business of producing crops and keeping animals and managing related agricultural activities.

Agribusiness — business activities connected with agricultural inputs, production, processing, transport, storage and marketing.

Weather — the atmospheric condition at a particular place and time.

Climate — the long-term pattern of weather of a place.

Irrigation — artificial application of water to crops.

Drainage — removal of excess water from land or soil.

Soil texture — relative proportion of sand, silt and clay particles in soil.

Soil structure — arrangement of soil particles into aggregates.

Soil fertility — ability of soil to supply plants with nutrients in suitable amounts.

Weathering — breakdown or alteration of rocks at or near the earth's surface.

Soil erosion — removal and transport of soil by agents such as water and wind.

Mulching — covering the soil surface with suitable material.

Crop rotation — planned sequence of different crops on the same land over successive seasons.

Monoculture — production dominated by one crop on a piece of land.

Livestock — domesticated animals kept for useful products or services.

Depreciation — decrease in value of an asset over time because of use, age, wear or obsolescence.

Revenue — money received from sales.

Profit — revenue minus total costs.

## Important comparisons

### Weather versus climate
Weather is short-term atmospheric condition; climate is the long-term pattern.

### Sandy versus clay soil
Sandy soil has larger particles and usually drains quickly. Clay has very small particles and usually holds more water but may drain slowly.

### Manure versus fertiliser
Manure is an organic material such as decomposed animal waste; fertiliser is a nutrient-containing material applied to supply plant nutrients. Both must be managed appropriately.

### Irrigation versus drainage
Irrigation adds water to crops; drainage removes excess water.

### Mixed versus specialised farming
Mixed farming combines crop and animal production; specialised farming concentrates mainly on one enterprise.

### Subsistence versus commercial farming
Subsistence production is mainly for household needs; commercial production is mainly for sale.

### Tool versus implement versus machinery
A tool is generally hand-operated; an implement is equipment used for a specific farm operation, often with a power source; machinery generally has powered moving parts.

## Soil erosion: causes, effects and control
Causes: vegetation removal, overgrazing, bare soil, cultivation on unsuitable slopes, uncontrolled runoff and strong winds.

Effects: loss of topsoil, reduced fertility, reduced yields, gullying, siltation and land degradation.

Control: contouring, grass strips, mulching, cover crops, terracing where suitable, controlled grazing, windbreaks and maintaining vegetation.

## Crop production sequence
1. Select suitable crop and seed.
2. Choose suitable site.
3. Prepare land.
4. Plant at suitable time, depth and spacing.
5. Manage moisture and nutrients.
6. Control weeds.
7. Monitor pests and diseases.
8. Thin or gap-fill where necessary.
9. Harvest at suitable maturity.
10. Clean, grade, dry and store.
11. Process or market where appropriate.
12. Evaluate the enterprise.

## Livestock production sequence
1. Choose suitable enterprise.
2. Select healthy animals.
3. Prepare housing.
4. Provide adequate feed and clean water.
5. Maintain hygiene.
6. Prevent and control disease and parasites.
7. Manage breeding.
8. Keep records.
9. Harvest or sell products.
10. Evaluate production and profitability.

## Agribusiness calculation skills
Revenue = quantity sold × price per unit.

Profit = total revenue − total costs.

If:
Quantity = 100 units
Price = $3 per unit
Revenue = $300.

If total costs = $220:
Profit = $300 − $220 = $80.

If costs exceed revenue, the result is a loss.

## Common examination command words
State — give the required fact briefly.
Name — provide the correct term or example.
Define — give the meaning of a term.
List — give several items.
Identify — recognise or point out the correct item.
Describe — give characteristics or steps.
Explain — give a reason or show how/why.
Compare — show similarities and/or differences.
Calculate — use the correct formula and show working.
Evaluate — judge the value or effectiveness using evidence.

## Practical skills checklist
A learner should be able to:
- identify common farm tools;
- use simple tools safely;
- clean and store tools;
- identify soil samples;
- demonstrate basic soil-conservation methods;
- demonstrate water conservation;
- establish or manage a small crop plot;
- identify weeds, pests and disease symptoms;
- describe livestock housing and feeding;
- keep basic agricultural records;
- prepare a simple enterprise budget;
- calculate revenue and profit/loss;
- explain how agricultural products can be processed and marketed.

## Short-answer practice
1. Define agriculture.
2. State four importance of agriculture.
3. Name four branches of agriculture.
4. Give two differences between weather and climate.
5. Name three sources of agricultural water.
6. Define irrigation.
7. State three methods of water conservation.
8. Define soil texture.
9. Name the three main soil particle classes.
10. State three causes of soil erosion.
11. Give four soil-conservation methods.
12. Define crop rotation.
13. State three conditions necessary for germination.
14. Give four methods of weed control.
15. Name three livestock products.
16. State four animal-health precautions.
17. Give three examples of farm implements.
18. State four tool-maintenance practices.
19. Define agribusiness.
20. Give the formula for profit.

## Structured-answer practice themes
A farmer has poor maize yields. Discuss possible causes and recommend solutions under climate, water, soil, crop management and enterprise management.

A school wants to establish a vegetable garden. Explain how learners could select the site, prepare the soil, plant, manage the crop, harvest, keep records and market the produce.

A farmer wants to keep poultry commercially. Discuss housing, feeding, water, hygiene, disease prevention, records, marketing, costs and income.

A community is experiencing severe soil erosion. Explain the causes, effects and practical conservation measures.

A farmer has limited water. Compare suitable water-conservation and irrigation strategies.

## Final revision strategy
Study definitions first, then processes and comparisons. Practise drawing simple diagrams such as soil profiles and farm layouts where required. For structured questions, organise answers using headings and numbered points. Where a question asks for a reason, do not merely list a term; explain the relationship. For calculations, write the formula, substitute values, calculate and give the correct unit where applicable.

Remember that Grade 7 Agriculture is practical as well as theoretical. Understanding how a farming activity works is more useful than memorising isolated words.

Topic 1: Introduction to Agriculture — meaning, importance, branches, farming systems, factors affecting production, health and safety, food security, sustainability.
Topic 2: Climate and Land Use — weather, climate, climate elements, Zimbabwe natural farming regions, land capability, climate hazards and adaptation.
Topic 3: Water — sources, quality, conservation, harvesting, irrigation, drainage, pollution, soil moisture and livestock water.
Topic 4: Soil — formation, weathering, profile, components, texture, structure, fertility, nutrients, manure, fertilisers, pH, erosion and conservation.
Topic 5: Plants — crop classes, seed, germination, nursery, land preparation, planting, crop management, weeds, pests, diseases, rotation, harvesting, post-harvest handling and value addition.
Topic 6: Animals — livestock enterprises, selection, housing, nutrition, pasture, health, diseases, parasites, breeding, welfare, products and records.
Topic 7: Farm Implements and Machinery — tools, implements, machinery, selection, animal traction, tractor operations, costs, maintenance, safety and technology.
Topic 8: Agribusiness — enterprises, enterprise selection, budgeting, costs, revenue, profit/loss, records, marketing, value addition, entrepreneurship, risk and technology.

CROSS-CUTTING THEMES: safety; health issues; food security; technology; environmental issues; disaster risk management; financial literacy; heritage.

topic: 1A. Farming Systems, Branches and Agricultural Development
source: Expanded Grade 7 Agriculture study notes based on the Junior Agriculture syllabus.
content:
# 1A. FARMING SYSTEMS, BRANCHES AND AGRICULTURAL DEVELOPMENT

## Agriculture as a system
A farm can be viewed as a system. Inputs such as land, labour, seed, feed, water, fertiliser, tools, capital and knowledge enter the system. Farming activities transform inputs into outputs such as crops, animals, manure and income. Good management aims to use resources efficiently while protecting the environment.

## Inputs in agriculture
Land provides the physical space and soil. Labour supplies human effort and skills. Capital provides money and equipment. Management involves planning and decision-making. Water and climate provide important natural conditions. Seed, livestock, fertiliser, feed and medicines are production inputs.

## Outputs
Outputs include food, fibre, livestock products, manure, income and employment. Some outputs can become inputs for another enterprise. For example, crop residues may become animal feed and manure may return nutrients to fields.

## Farming systems in more detail
### Subsistence system
The main objective is household consumption. Production decisions are strongly influenced by family food requirements. Surplus can be sold or exchanged.

### Commercial system
Production is planned for a market. The farmer considers demand, expected prices, production costs, quality standards, transport and profit.

### Mixed farming
Crops and livestock are produced together. Advantages include recycling manure, using crop residues as feed and spreading income sources. Disadvantages can include higher management demands and competition for resources.

### Diversified farming
Several enterprises reduce dependence on a single source of income. Diversification can also provide food at different times of the year.

### Specialised farming
Concentration on one enterprise may make management easier and allow specialised skills and equipment to be developed. The farmer may, however, face greater risk from a disease outbreak, drought or price fall affecting that enterprise.

### Integrated farming
Integration is stronger than simply having several enterprises. The enterprises are linked so that outputs or wastes from one are deliberately used as inputs by another.

## Branches and careers
Agriculture provides careers in crop science, animal science, veterinary work, agricultural engineering, extension, economics, agribusiness, research, irrigation, food processing, environmental management and farm management.

## Agriculture and national development
Agriculture contributes to food security, employment, industrial raw materials, rural development and trade. When farm productivity increases sustainably, more raw materials may become available for processing and more households can earn income.

## Constraints to agriculture
Common constraints include drought, pests, diseases, soil degradation, lack of capital, high input costs, poor roads, limited storage, inadequate markets, limited technical knowledge and climate variability.

## Ways of improving agriculture
Improvement can involve better extension, appropriate technology, improved seed, conservation, irrigation, training, market information, storage, processing and responsible use of inputs.

## Food security
Food security involves reliable access to adequate and nutritious food. At household level, food security can be strengthened through diversified production, home gardens, livestock, safe storage and income generation.

## Safety and responsibility
Agriculture is productive only when people and the environment are protected. Safe chemical handling, tool maintenance, livestock welfare, clean water and responsible waste disposal should be part of every enterprise.

topic: 2A. Climate, Natural Farming Regions and Agricultural Planning
source: Expanded Grade 7 Agriculture study notes based on the Junior Agriculture syllabus and Zimbabwe agricultural-region concepts.
content:
# 2A. CLIMATE, NATURAL FARMING REGIONS AND AGRICULTURAL PLANNING

## Climate and crop calendars
A crop calendar is a plan showing when land preparation, planting, weeding, pest monitoring and harvesting should occur. Farmers use rainfall patterns, temperature, crop maturity period and local experience when planning.

## Rainfall distribution
Two farms may receive similar annual rainfall but have different production results if one receives reliable rainfall throughout the growing season and the other receives long dry spells followed by heavy storms.

## Rainfall intensity
Gentle rainfall can infiltrate soil more effectively. Very intense rainfall may produce runoff and erosion, especially where soil is bare or compacted.

## Temperature and crop growth
Very low or very high temperatures can slow growth or damage crops. Germination, flowering and grain filling may each have different temperature requirements.

## Natural farming regions
Zimbabwe's natural farming regions are used to describe broad differences in rainfall and agricultural potential. They are useful for planning, but a farmer should also consider local soil, water, slope and management.

Region I is generally associated with high rainfall and high agricultural potential.
Region II generally has relatively favourable rainfall and supports intensive crop and livestock enterprises where soils and other conditions permit.
Region III has more pronounced dry periods and greater drought risk; farming systems need careful water and risk management.
Region IV has low and unreliable rainfall and is more suited to drought-adapted enterprises and irrigation where water is available.
Region V has very low and unreliable rainfall in much of its area and supports extensive livestock, wildlife and other activities adapted to dry conditions.

## Land capability
Land capability means the suitability of land for particular uses without causing unacceptable degradation. Steep land may require stronger conservation measures. Waterlogged land may need drainage or may be unsuitable for some crops. Shallow soils may limit rooting depth.

## Land-use conflicts
Agriculture can compete with settlements, industry, roads, conservation and other uses. Planning should reduce conflicts and protect productive agricultural land and sensitive environments.

## Climate adaptation
Farmers can adapt by:
- selecting suitable crops and varieties;
- adjusting planting dates;
- conserving soil moisture;
- harvesting water;
- using irrigation where feasible;
- maintaining crop residues or mulch;
- conserving fodder;
- adjusting livestock numbers;
- diversifying enterprises.

## Drought preparedness
Before a drought, farmers can maintain water-storage facilities, conserve fodder, plan livestock numbers, plant suitable crops and protect soil cover. During drought, water and feed should be prioritised and unnecessary losses reduced.

## Flood preparedness
Maintain drainage, avoid blocking waterways, protect riverbanks, maintain vegetation and avoid establishing vulnerable enterprises in flood-prone locations.

## Farm planning
A farm plan can show fields, gardens, livestock units, water sources, roads, buildings, storage, waste areas and conservation structures. The plan should place enterprises where their requirements can be met safely and efficiently.

topic: 3A. Water Conservation, Irrigation and Practical Water Management
source: Expanded Grade 7 Agriculture study notes based on the Junior Agriculture syllabus.
content:
# 3A. WATER CONSERVATION, IRRIGATION AND PRACTICAL WATER MANAGEMENT

## Why water must be managed
Water is a limited resource. Agriculture can use large quantities, so farmers must apply enough for production without wasting it or causing waterlogging, salinity, erosion or pollution.

## Water harvesting examples
### Roof harvesting
Rain falling on a roof is directed through gutters into a tank. The water can be used for suitable agricultural activities after appropriate safety considerations.

### Runoff harvesting
Runoff can be directed into suitable storage structures or infiltration areas. Structures must be properly designed to avoid dangerous erosion or collapse.

### Small reservoirs and ponds
These store water for later use. They need protection from contamination, excessive evaporation and unsafe access.

## Irrigation scheduling
Irrigation should consider crop stage, soil moisture, weather, soil type and available water. Over-irrigation wastes water and can cause waterlogging; under-irrigation causes crop stress.

## Irrigation efficiency
Efficient systems deliver water where it is needed with minimal losses. Drip irrigation can reduce evaporation and runoff when correctly installed. Sprinklers can provide relatively uniform application. Surface systems may be appropriate where conditions and water supply permit.

## Waterlogging
Waterlogging occurs when soil remains excessively saturated. It reduces air spaces and can suffocate roots. Symptoms can include poor growth, yellowing and root damage.

## Drainage
Drainage removes excess water. Open drains may be used in some fields; other systems use underground drainage where justified. Drainage structures must be maintained so they do not become blocked.

## Water pollution from farms
Pollution can come from excessive fertiliser, pesticide misuse, animal waste, soil sediment, fuel and rubbish. Pollution can harm aquatic organisms, animals and people.

## Protecting water sources
Keep livestock from damaging sensitive banks, maintain vegetation near waterways where appropriate, dispose of waste safely and avoid storing chemicals close to water.

## Practical investigation
A learner can compare two pieces of land after rainfall and observe infiltration, runoff and erosion. The observations can be recorded in a table with date, rainfall condition, soil condition, runoff and visible erosion.

## Water-saving garden practices
Use mulch, plant at appropriate times, remove competing weeds, maintain healthy soil organic matter, repair leaks and water plants efficiently.

## Safe water use
Never assume that water is safe to drink simply because it looks clean. Drinking-water safety is a health issue and should follow appropriate public-health guidance.

content:
# 4A. SOIL PROPERTIES, FERTILITY AND CONSERVATION

## Physical properties
Texture, structure, colour, depth, drainage and water-holding capacity are important physical properties.

## Texture by feel
A sandy soil feels gritty because of larger particles. Clay has very fine particles and can feel smooth or sticky when wet. Loam has a mixture of particle sizes.

## Structure and aggregates
Well-formed aggregates create spaces for air and water. Organic matter and biological activity can support stable soil aggregates.

## Soil organisms
Earthworms create channels and contribute to mixing organic material. Microorganisms decompose organic matter and participate in nutrient cycling.

## Organic matter
Organic matter improves soil condition by supporting aggregation, moisture retention and biological activity. It also releases nutrients as it decomposes.

## Essential nutrients
Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are major nutrients required in relatively large amounts. Calcium, magnesium and sulphur are also important, while micronutrients are needed in smaller quantities.

## Nutrient deficiency
Deficiency can cause poor growth, abnormal leaf colour, weak plants or poor yield. Diagnosis should consider the whole plant and growing environment rather than assuming every symptom is caused by one nutrient.

## Fertiliser management
Fertilisers should be selected and applied according to crop and soil needs. Excessive application can waste money and contribute to water pollution.

## Manure management
Fresh manure can contain weed seeds or pathogens and may be unsuitable for immediate application in some situations. Proper composting or decomposition can improve handling and reduce some risks.

## Soil acidity
Very acidic soil can reduce availability of some nutrients and affect roots and soil organisms. Liming is used in appropriate circumstances to raise pH.

## Erosion by water
Raindrops can detach particles, while flowing water transports them. Bare and sloping land is especially vulnerable.

## Wind erosion
Strong winds can move fine dry soil particles. Windbreaks, shelterbelts, crop cover and maintaining residues can reduce exposure.

## Conservation structures
Contour-based structures reduce the speed of water flowing downhill. Terraces can shorten slope length where appropriate. Grass strips and vegetation can trap sediment.

## Conservation agriculture principles
Common principles include minimum soil disturbance, maintaining soil cover and crop diversification. The exact practices should be adapted to local conditions.

## Practical soil investigation
Collect representative samples, label them, compare texture and observe colour and organic matter. Avoid making a fertiliser recommendation from an untested sample when laboratory soil testing is available.

## Soil conservation project
A school can map erosion-prone areas, identify causes, install suitable conservation measures and monitor changes after rainfall.

content:
# 5A. CROP PRODUCTION, PEST CONTROL AND POST-HARVEST MANAGEMENT

## Seed quality
High-quality seed should be viable, clean, healthy and suited to the crop and environment. Poor seed can produce uneven stands and low yields.

## Germination sequence
Under suitable conditions, the seed absorbs water, metabolic activity increases and the embryo begins growth. The root emerges first in many common crop seeds, followed by shoot development.

## Nursery management
A nursery should have suitable growing medium, drainage, water and protection. Overcrowding can encourage disease and produce weak seedlings.

## Transplanting
Seedlings should be handled carefully. Transplanting is best done under suitable moisture and weather conditions to reduce transplant shock.

## Spacing
Correct spacing reduces excessive competition and can improve light interception and airflow. The ideal spacing depends on crop and production system.

## Weed management
Weeds compete with crops and may harbour pests and diseases. Early control is often important because young crops are vulnerable to competition.

## Cultural pest control
Practices include crop rotation, timely planting, field sanitation, resistant varieties and removal of crop residues that harbour pests.

## Biological control
Beneficial organisms can suppress pests. Biological methods should be understood as part of an integrated strategy rather than assuming every insect is harmful.

## Chemical control
Pesticides can be useful but must be used responsibly and according to the product label and applicable regulations. Learners should never handle hazardous chemicals without appropriate adult supervision and protection.

## Disease management
Healthy planting material, sanitation, suitable spacing, crop rotation and resistant varieties can reduce disease pressure.

## Integrated pest management
IPM combines monitoring, prevention, cultural, mechanical, biological and carefully selected chemical methods. The aim is effective control with reduced unnecessary pesticide use.

## Harvest maturity
Signs of maturity differ among crops. Harvesting at the correct stage helps preserve quality and reduce losses.

## Storage
Grain should be sufficiently dry before safe storage. Storage areas should be clean, dry, protected from pests and suitable for the product.

## Post-harvest loss
Loss can occur through insects, rodents, mould, moisture, mechanical damage and poor handling. Good drying, grading, packaging and storage reduce loss.

## Value addition
Value addition may include cleaning, grading, milling, drying, processing and packaging. It can create employment and improve returns.

## Crop rotation planning
A simple rotation can alternate cereals with legumes and include other suitable crops. Rotation should consider local climate, soil and enterprise objectives.

## Farm records
Record planting date, seed source, area planted, labour, inputs, rainfall observations, pest events, harvest quantity, sales and costs.

content:
# 6A. LIVESTOCK FEEDING, HOUSING, HEALTH AND RECORDS

## Animal needs
Animals require suitable feed, water, shelter, space, health care and management. Requirements vary with species, age, body size and production stage.

## Feed classes
Feeds can be broadly considered as energy feeds, protein-rich feeds, roughages, minerals and vitamin sources. Many feeds provide more than one nutrient.

## Ration
A ration is the quantity and combination of feed supplied to an animal over a specified period. A good ration should be appropriate to the animal's needs and economically practical.

## Water
Water must be clean and readily accessible. Hot conditions and milk production can increase water needs.

## Housing
Housing protects animals from weather, predators and injury and makes management easier. Good housing should have ventilation, drainage, hygiene, adequate space and appropriate floors.

## Poultry housing
Poultry houses should protect birds from rain, excessive heat, predators and disease. Litter should be kept reasonably dry and contaminated material removed.

## Cattle, goat and sheep management
Ruminants need appropriate forage and supplementary feed where necessary. Grazing should be managed to prevent overstocking and pasture degradation.

## Pig management
Pigs need clean housing, adequate water, balanced feed and good sanitation. Waste should be managed to reduce pollution and disease.

## Rabbit management
Rabbits need secure housing, suitable feed, clean water and protection from extreme conditions. Housing should permit cleaning and safe handling.

## Disease transmission
Disease may spread through direct animal contact, contaminated feed or water, equipment, people, insects and other vectors.

## Biosecurity
Biosecurity means measures that reduce the introduction and spread of disease. Examples include quarantine of new animals where appropriate, sanitation, controlling visitors and separating sick animals.

## Parasites
External parasites can irritate animals and may transmit disease. Internal parasites can reduce growth and production. Control should be based on appropriate veterinary guidance.

## Animal welfare
Animals should be handled humanely. Avoid unnecessary pain, fear, hunger, thirst and injury. Provide appropriate shelter, feed, water and health care.

## Breeding records
Record mating dates, parentage, births, deaths and production. Records help identify productive animals and improve management.

## Product hygiene
Milk, eggs and meat can become contaminated. Clean handling, appropriate storage and hygienic production protect consumers.

## Simple livestock budget
Costs may include purchase of stock, feed, medicines, housing, labour and transport. Income may come from sales of animals or products.

## Practical livestock project
Learners can observe a local enterprise and record species, housing type, feed sources, water source, health measures, products and marketing method. They should not handle animals or medicines without appropriate supervision.

content:
# 7A. FARM TOOLS, IMPLEMENTS, MACHINERY AND MAINTENANCE

## Hand tools
Hoe: loosening soil, making planting holes and weeding.
Spade: digging and moving soil.
Fork: handling manure and loose materials.
Rake: levelling soil and collecting debris.
Slasher: cutting grass and vegetation.
Secateurs: pruning small branches.
Pruning saw: cutting larger branches.
Wheelbarrow: moving materials over short distances.

## Correct tool selection
Use the tool designed for the job. A wrong tool can reduce efficiency, damage the crop or cause injury.

## Tool condition
Handles should be firm and free from dangerous cracks. Metal parts should be secure. Cutting tools should be kept appropriately sharp.

## Implements
Plough: used for primary tillage in suitable conditions.
Harrow: breaks clods and prepares the seedbed.
Planter or seeder: places seed at controlled depth and spacing.
Cultivator: loosens soil between rows and can control weeds.
Ridger: forms ridges where suitable.
Sprayer: applies liquids such as pesticides or other agricultural products.

## Animal-drawn equipment
Animal-drawn ploughs and cultivators use draught power. Animals must be healthy, properly trained and adequately fed and watered.

## Tractor safety
Only trained operators should use tractors. Keep children and unnecessary people away from operating machinery. Never perform maintenance on moving machinery.

## Maintenance schedule
Daily: clean, inspect, check obvious damage and lubricate where required.
Periodic: tighten fasteners, service engines according to instructions, inspect tyres and replace worn parts.
Long-term: store equipment under cover and protect against rust and weather.

## Storage
Tools should be arranged so that users can identify and retrieve them safely. Sharp tools should not be left where someone can step on them or accidentally touch the blade.

## Tool inventory
A school agriculture department can keep a tool register containing tool name, number available, condition, location, date issued and return status.

## Economic decision: buy or hire
Buying may be justified where equipment is used frequently and ownership costs are affordable. Hiring may be cheaper for occasional operations. The decision should consider total cost, availability and timing.

## Environmental considerations
Heavy machinery can compact soil if used excessively or under unsuitable conditions. Fuel spills and waste oils can pollute soil and water. Proper handling and maintenance are essential.

content:
# 8A. AGRIBUSINESS PLANNING, BUDGETING, MARKETING AND PROFIT

## Enterprise planning
Before starting, define the product, customer, resources, production method, expected costs, expected selling price and risks.

## Opportunity identification
An opportunity exists when there is a need that can be met with a product or service. A school might identify demand for vegetable seedlings, fresh vegetables, eggs or another locally suitable product.

## Simple business plan
A simple plan contains:
1. enterprise name;
2. product;
3. target customers;
4. resources required;
5. production steps;
6. estimated costs;
7. expected output;
8. expected selling price;
9. marketing method;
10. risks and solutions.

## Cost categories
Variable costs change with production level. Examples are seed, feed, fertiliser, packaging and some hired labour.

Fixed costs do not change directly with short-term output. Examples can include some buildings and equipment.

## Revenue
Revenue is the value of sales.

Revenue = Quantity sold × Price.

If 80 trays are sold at $2.50 each:
Revenue = 80 × 2.50 = $200.

## Profit
Profit = Revenue − Total costs.

If revenue is $200 and total costs are $140:
Profit = $60.

## Break-even idea
Break-even is the point at which total revenue equals total cost. At break-even, there is neither profit nor loss.

## Record keeping
Records should be accurate, dated and kept consistently. Separate personal spending from enterprise money when possible.

## Stock records
Record quantities of seed, feed, fertiliser, chemicals, packaging and finished products. Stock records help prevent shortages and unexplained losses.

## Pricing
A farmer must consider production costs, market prices, quality, demand, transport, packaging and competition. A price that is too low may fail to cover costs; a price that is too high may reduce sales.

## Marketing channels
Farmers may sell directly to consumers, through local markets, traders, shops, cooperatives or processors. The best channel depends on quantity, quality, location and transaction costs.

## Grading
Grading separates produce according to quality, size, maturity or other characteristics. It can help buyers compare products and may improve returns.

## Packaging
Packaging protects products, improves handling and can provide information. Packaging should be suitable for the product and market.

## Value addition
Processing can increase shelf life and convenience. Examples include drying, milling, preserving, making juice, grading and packaging.

## Entrepreneurship
An entrepreneur identifies opportunities, plans, takes calculated risks, manages resources and evaluates results.

## Enterprise evaluation
At the end, compare planned and actual:
- costs;
- yield;
- sales;
- price;
- revenue;
- profit;
- labour;
- losses.

Then identify improvements for the next cycle.

## Agricultural risk
Risks include drought, floods, pests, diseases, theft, fire and price changes. Diversification, good husbandry, safe storage, conservation and market research can reduce some risks.

content:
# GRADE 7 AGRICULTURE EXAMINATION AND PRACTICAL MASTERCLASS

## Assessment structure context
The Junior Agriculture syllabus describes multiple-choice and structured assessment alongside continuous assessment. Later competency-based Grade 7 examination arrangements combine Agriculture with Science and Technology/ICT under Agriculture, Science and Technology. The Agriculture learning area remains a major component, so learners should prepare both knowledge and application.

## Multiple-choice strategy
Read the entire question before choosing an answer. Look for key words such as NOT, BEST, MAIN, FIRST and MOST suitable. Eliminate clearly wrong answers before choosing between the remaining options.

## Structured-question strategy
For “state” questions, give concise facts.
For “describe” questions, provide characteristics or a sequence.
For “explain” questions, give a cause-and-effect relationship.
For “compare” questions, show differences or similarities.
For “calculate” questions, show the formula and working.

## Practical observation
If shown a tool, soil sample, crop, livestock structure or farm situation:
1. identify it;
2. state its use;
3. explain safe handling;
4. give maintenance or management requirements;
5. relate it to the agricultural enterprise.

## Soil practical
Possible observations include texture, colour, structure, moisture, organic matter and profile layers. Always distinguish observation from conclusion.

## Crop practical
Be able to recognise stages such as germination, seedling growth, vegetative growth, flowering and maturity. Identify common management activities such as weeding, thinning, gap filling, mulching and irrigation.

## Livestock practical
Identify housing features, feed, water, hygiene measures and possible signs of poor health. Avoid diagnosing disease solely from one symptom; appropriate veterinary advice is needed.

## Tools practical
Identify a tool, state its use, demonstrate safe handling and explain cleaning, sharpening, storage and maintenance.

## Agribusiness practical
Given quantity, selling price and costs:
Revenue = quantity × unit price.
Profit = revenue − total costs.

Always distinguish an expense from a sale.

## Sample integrated scenario
A school has a small piece of land, limited water and a nearby market.

A strong answer should:
- select a suitable enterprise;
- consider climate and soil;
- conserve water;
- choose appropriate seed;
- prepare land;
- plan spacing;
- manage weeds and pests;
- keep records;
- calculate costs;
- harvest correctly;
- grade and package;
- market the product;
- calculate profit or loss;
- evaluate environmental sustainability.

## Common errors
Do not confuse weather with climate.
Do not confuse irrigation with drainage.
Do not confuse soil texture with structure.
Do not call every insect a pest.
Do not recommend excessive fertiliser without considering soil and crop needs.
Do not ignore safety when discussing tools or chemicals.
Do not calculate profit without subtracting total costs.

## Revision checklist
Can you define all major terms?
Can you explain the eight topics?
Can you compare farming systems?
Can you explain Zimbabwe's broad natural farming regions?
Can you describe water conservation?
Can you explain soil erosion?
Can you outline crop production from seed to market?
Can you explain livestock feeding and health?
Can you identify farm tools and their uses?
Can you prepare a simple farm budget?
Can you calculate revenue and profit?
Can you explain value addition?
Can you apply agriculture knowledge to a local farming problem?

# APPLIED AGRICULTURE CASE STUDIES AND PROBLEM SOLVING

## Case 1: Poor crop stand
A field has many gaps after planting.
Possible causes include poor seed viability, poor planting depth, pests, drought, waterlogging, poor seed-soil contact or damage by animals.
A good investigation should identify evidence before selecting a solution.
Possible responses include better seed selection, correct planting depth, gap filling, moisture management, pest monitoring and improved land preparation.

## Case 2: Low maize yield
Possible causes include inadequate rainfall, nutrient deficiency, weeds, pests, diseases, poor seed, late planting, low plant population or soil erosion.
Do not assume that one cause is responsible. Examine climate, soil, crop management and farm records.

## Case 3: Vegetable garden with limited water
Choose crops according to available water, mulch the soil, control weeds, repair leaks, harvest rainwater where possible and use efficient irrigation. Planting should be planned so water is available during critical growth stages.

## Case 4: Severe soil erosion
Identify whether water or wind is the main agent. Examine slope, vegetation cover, tillage direction and runoff pathways. Select suitable measures such as contouring, grass strips, mulching, cover crops, windbreaks and controlled grazing.

## Case 5: Livestock losing weight
Possible causes include inadequate feed, poor-quality pasture, parasites, disease, insufficient water or overcrowding. Check feed and water, observe animals, review records and seek veterinary assistance where disease is suspected.

## Case 6: Poultry deaths
Possible causes include disease, poor ventilation, contaminated water, overcrowding, poor nutrition, extreme temperatures or predators. Isolate sick birds where appropriate, improve hygiene and seek veterinary guidance.

## Case 7: Farm enterprise making a loss
Compare planned and actual costs, yield, selling price and losses. The solution may involve reducing avoidable costs, improving productivity, changing the market, adding value or changing the enterprise.

## Problem-solving sequence
1. Identify the problem.
2. Collect observations.
3. Identify possible causes.
4. Compare alternatives.
5. Choose an appropriate response.
6. Implement safely.
7. Record the result.
8. Evaluate and improve.

Agriculture questions often reward answers that connect several topics rather than treating each topic as isolated.

content:
# WEATHER OBSERVATION, RECORDS AND AGRICULTURAL DECISIONS

## Weather records
A simple school weather record may include date, rainfall, temperature observation, cloud cover, wind condition and notable events.

## Why records matter
Records help learners recognise patterns and help farmers make decisions about planting, irrigation and pest monitoring.

## Rainfall records
Rainfall can be measured with a rain gauge. Measurements should be taken consistently and recorded with dates.

## Temperature observations
Temperature affects germination and crop growth. Simple maximum and minimum observations can help learners understand daily variation.

## Using records
A sequence of dry days may indicate a need to monitor crop moisture. Heavy rainfall may indicate a need to inspect erosion and drainage structures.

## Limitations
A school weather station represents its own location. It should not automatically be assumed to represent the entire district.

## Record presentation
Tables should have headings and units. Graphs can help reveal trends, but the learner should still explain what the trend means for agriculture.

## Link to farm planning
Weather records can be combined with planting dates, crop stages and yields to help evaluate which conditions were associated with better performance.

content:
# SOIL SAMPLING, SOIL TESTS AND FERTILITY DECISIONS

## Why test soil?
Soil testing can provide information about properties such as pH and nutrient status. This helps farmers avoid applying nutrients blindly.

## Sampling
Samples should represent the area being tested. Avoid unusual spots such as manure piles, roadsides or waterlogged patches unless they are being investigated separately.

## Soil texture
Texture affects drainage, water holding and nutrient retention. Texture generally changes slowly compared with soil nutrient levels.

## Soil fertility
Fertility can be improved by organic matter management, crop rotation, legumes, manure and appropriate fertilisers.

## Fertiliser decision
A responsible decision considers the crop, soil test results where available, expected yield, nutrient source, application method, cost and environmental risk.

## Organic matter
Compost and well-managed manure can improve soil physical condition and nutrient cycling.

## Avoiding nutrient loss
Excessive irrigation and heavy rainfall can move soluble nutrients beyond the root zone. Erosion can physically remove nutrient-rich topsoil.

## School practical
Compare soils from two sites. Record colour, texture by feel, visible organic matter and drainage condition. Discuss why the sites may support different crops.

topic: Weeds, Pests and Diseases: Identification and Integrated Control
source: Expanded Grade 7 Agriculture study notes based on the Junior Agriculture syllabus.
content:
# WEEDS, PESTS AND DISEASES

## Weeds
A weed is a plant growing where it is unwanted. Weeds compete with crops and can harbour pests.

## Weed-control methods
Hand pulling, hoeing, mulching, crop competition, crop rotation and suitable herbicide use are possible methods. Choice depends on crop, growth stage, scale and safety.

## Pests
Pests can chew leaves, bore into stems, attack roots, suck plant sap or damage stored products.

## Pest monitoring
Regular inspection helps detect problems early. Look at leaves, stems, roots, flowers and stored produce.

## Diseases
Disease symptoms may include spots, rotting, wilting, stunting, abnormal colour and dieback. A symptom is an observable sign, not necessarily a complete diagnosis.

## Integrated management
Use prevention first where possible. Combine sanitation, crop rotation, resistant varieties, appropriate spacing, biological control, mechanical control and carefully selected chemical control.

## Safe chemical practice
Only trained adults should handle hazardous agricultural chemicals. Follow the product label, use required protective equipment and keep chemicals away from children, food and water sources.

## Storage pests
Stored grain can be damaged by insects and rodents. Dry grain, clean stores, sealed containers where appropriate and regular inspection can reduce losses.

# LIVESTOCK RECORDS, BREEDING AND ENTERPRISE EVALUATION

## Identification
Animals can be identified using appropriate marks, tags or records. Identification helps trace health, breeding and production information.

## Breeding records
Record parentage, mating dates, births, offspring numbers and important reproductive information.

## Production records
Depending on enterprise, record eggs, milk, growth, live weights, sales or other outputs.

## Health records
Record vaccinations, treatments, illness, deaths and veterinary interventions.

## Feed records
Record type and quantity of feed where practical. Feed can be one of the major enterprise costs.

## Evaluation
Compare output with costs. A productive animal is not necessarily profitable if its costs are excessive.

## Culling
Culling means removing animals from the breeding or production enterprise according to defined criteria. Decisions should be based on health, performance, age, fertility and enterprise objectives.

## Enterprise improvement
Use records to select better-performing animals, identify recurring health problems, control costs and plan future production.

# FARM TOOL IDENTIFICATION AND PRACTICAL MAINTENANCE

## Hoe
Use: digging, loosening soil and weeding.
Maintenance: clean soil after use, dry the metal and store safely.

## Spade
Use: digging and moving soil.
Maintenance: keep blade clean and handle secure.

## Fork
Use: moving manure, compost or loose plant material.
Maintenance: clean tines and check handle.

## Rake
Use: levelling soil and collecting debris.
Maintenance: keep teeth secure and store under cover.

## Slasher
Use: cutting grass and vegetation.
Maintenance: keep blade appropriately sharp, protect the cutting edge and store safely.

## Secateurs
Use: pruning small branches.
Maintenance: clean blades, lubricate moving parts and store safely.

## Wheelbarrow
Use: transporting soil, manure, tools or produce.
Maintenance: check wheel, handles, tray and fasteners.

## Safety
Carry tools with points and blades controlled. Never leave sharp tools on paths. Wear suitable footwear and protective clothing.

## Practical examination
When shown a tool, answer in this order: name → use → safety precaution → maintenance practice.

# AGRICULTURAL MARKETING AND VALUE ADDITION

## Market
A market is a place or system where buyers and sellers exchange goods or services.

## Market research
Ask what customers want, when they want it, what quality they expect and what they are willing to pay.

## Product quality
Quality may involve freshness, size, cleanliness, maturity, uniformity and absence of damage.

## Grading
Grading separates products into groups according to defined quality characteristics.

## Packaging
Packaging protects products and can make handling easier. It can also communicate product information.

## Value addition
Value can be added by cleaning, grading, drying, milling, processing or packaging.

## Transport
Transport affects cost and product quality. Perishable products need careful handling and timely movement.

## Price
Price is influenced by supply, demand, quality, season, competition, transport and processing.

## Direct selling
Selling directly can allow a farmer to receive a larger share of the consumer price but may require more time and marketing effort.

## Cooperatives
Farmers can sometimes work together to buy inputs, market produce or share facilities. Cooperation can improve bargaining power where properly managed.

# FINANCIAL LITERACY FOR AGRICULTURAL ENTERPRISES

## Budget
A budget is a plan of expected income and expenditure.

## Cash flow
Cash flow concerns money entering and leaving the enterprise over time. An enterprise can be profitable but temporarily short of cash if sales occur later than expenses.

## Unit cost
Unit cost can be estimated as:
Total cost ÷ quantity produced.

## Gross and net ideas
Revenue is sales income. Net profit is what remains after all relevant costs are considered.

## Saving
Saving part of income can help finance future inputs or unexpected needs.

## Separating records
Keep enterprise records separate from personal spending where possible. This makes evaluation more accurate.

## Example
If total cost is $300 and 150 units are produced:
Unit cost = $300 ÷ 150 = $2 per unit.
If sold for $2.80 each, the margin before other unrecorded costs is $0.80 per unit.

## Financial decisions
Before borrowing or investing, consider expected return, repayment obligations, risk and whether the enterprise can generate enough income.

# ENVIRONMENTAL MANAGEMENT AND SUSTAINABLE AGRICULTURE

## Sustainable production
Sustainable agriculture protects the productive capacity of land and water while meeting current needs.

## Soil
Protect soil from erosion, maintain organic matter and avoid unnecessary disturbance.

## Water
Prevent pollution, conserve water and maintain suitable drainage.

## Vegetation
Trees, grasses and other vegetation can reduce erosion, provide habitats and protect waterways.

## Biodiversity
A diverse agricultural environment can support beneficial organisms and improve resilience. Farmers should distinguish beneficial organisms from pests.

## Waste management
Waste should be reduced, reused where safe and disposed of responsibly. Animal manure can be useful when properly managed.

## Chemical responsibility
Use agricultural chemicals only when necessary, according to approved instructions and with appropriate protection. Avoid contamination of food, people and water.

## Climate resilience
Diversification, water conservation, soil cover, drought-tolerant crops and appropriate livestock management can improve resilience.

## Disaster risk management
Identify hazards, assess vulnerability, prepare prevention measures and plan responses. Agriculture can be affected by drought, floods, storms, fire, pests and diseases.
